inputs.need:
I am an obstetric physician at a regional maternity unit with about 5,200 births a year. Women with pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension are discharged two or three days after birth, and their blood pressure is then checked by community midwives around day five and at the six-week visit with the family doctor. Blood pressure often peaks in the first week after birth, and we see women readmitted with severe hypertension or headaches, and rarely strokes, sometimes because nobody measured their pressure between visits or because their medicines were not adjusted. Last year 38 women were readmitted within six weeks with postpartum hypertension.

The hospital charity has funded home blood pressure monitors and a simple app: women would measure their blood pressure twice a day for two weeks and then daily to six weeks, with readings sent to a midwife-led hub that adjusts antihypertensive medicines by a written protocol and calls women with high readings. We want to run a pragmatic trial comparing remote monitoring with the usual community checks, in the real conditions of our service, with our own midwives rather than research staff.

I need help choosing an outcome that matters to women and that we can measure well (severe hypertension, readmission, or blood pressure control at six weeks), estimating the sample size with our numbers, and making sure that women who do not own a smartphone or who speak little English are not excluded. We would also like to hear what women think of measuring their own blood pressure with a newborn at home.
inputs.constraints: Charity funding covers 300 monitors and the app licence for 18 months. The midwife hub runs from 08:00 to 20:00; high readings out of hours go to the maternity assessment unit. No extra clinic visits for trial purposes.

records.title: Remote blood pressure monitoring after hypertensive pregnancy: a pragmatic trial in two maternity units
records.authors: Nkemelu-Forsberg A, Castellano-Hart D, Iwu-Lindqvist P
records.abstract: We allocated 440 women discharged after a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy to remote blood pressure monitoring with text-message reporting or to usual community checks. Blood pressure was recorded between days 3 and 10 in 92 percent of women with remote monitoring and 44 percent with usual care. Readmission for hypertension within six weeks was 3.1 percent with remote monitoring and 4.0 percent with usual care, a difference the trial was not powered to detect. Women in the remote arm more often had their medicines reduced before six weeks. Most women found remote monitoring reassuring. The trial excluded women without a smartphone.

records.title: Timing of peak blood pressure after pre-eclampsia and gestational hypertension
records.abstract: We reviewed twice-daily blood pressure readings for 356 women with pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension during the first two weeks after birth, from inpatient charts and home readings. Blood pressure peaked between days 3 and 6 after birth in 71 percent of women, often after discharge. Women with pre-eclampsia and those who had stopped antihypertensive medicine before discharge had the highest peaks. Severe readings of 160 over 110 or more occurred in 14 percent of women, most at home. Home readings were taken on devices of different makes, and some women stopped recording after the first week.

records.title: Self-management of postpartum hypertension with home monitoring and medication titration: blood pressure at six weeks
records.abstract: Women with postpartum hypertension were allocated to self-management, with home monitoring and medication titration by a written protocol, or to usual care. Mean diastolic blood pressure at six weeks was 5 mmHg lower with self-management, and blood pressure below 140 over 90 at six weeks was reached by 76 percent of women with self-management and 61 percent with usual care. Fewer women in the self-management group were still taking antihypertensive medicine at six weeks. The trial was small and conducted in one hospital, and women who agreed to take part were more often educated beyond school.

records.title: Readmission for postpartum hypertension: incidence and predictors in a regional population
records.abstract: Using regional hospital records for 9,820 women with a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, we examined readmission for hypertension within six weeks of birth. Readmission occurred in 7 percent of women and was more common after pre-eclampsia, in women aged over 35 and in women discharged without antihypertensive medicine despite high readings. Most readmissions occurred within ten days of birth. Readmitted women stayed a median of two nights. The records did not show whether blood pressure had been measured between discharge and readmission, so missed opportunities could not be counted.

records.title: Digital exclusion in postpartum remote monitoring programmes
records.abstract: We examined who took part in a postpartum remote blood pressure monitoring programme offered to all eligible women in three maternity units. Twelve percent of eligible women did not own a smartphone. Uptake of remote monitoring was 58 percent among women who needed an interpreter and 86 percent among other women. Offering a loan phone and a paper diary with phone calls from the hub raised uptake among women without a smartphone to 71 percent. Women living in the most deprived areas submitted readings on fewer days. Programmes that rely on a smartphone app alone risk widening inequalities in postpartum care.

records.title: Women's experiences of measuring their own blood pressure with a newborn at home
records.abstract: We held semi-structured conversations with 22 women who monitored their own blood pressure after a hypertensive pregnancy. Women described feeling reassured and in control, but found twice-daily readings hard to fit around feeding and broken sleep, especially in the first week. Several women said that a call from a midwife after a high reading made them feel looked after rather than alarmed. Women with other young children and those without a partner at home found monitoring hardest. Most women wanted to stop monitoring once readings were stable. Participants were recruited from one programme and were mostly fluent in English.

records.title: Accuracy of automated home blood pressure monitors in postpartum women
records.abstract: We compared three automated upper-arm home blood pressure monitors with observer measurements in 180 postpartum women. Two monitors met accuracy standards, with mean differences within 5 mmHg for systolic and diastolic pressure, while the third underestimated systolic pressure by about 8 mmHg at high readings. Accuracy was similar in women with and without pre-eclampsia. Correct cuff size mattered more than monitor model. We recommend using only monitors validated in pregnancy and the postpartum period and checking cuff size at the first use.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; the three leads remain unverified and are not part of the certainty. Remote monitoring closes the measurement gap in the first ten days, and self-management with protocol titration improved blood pressure control at six weeks in a small trial, while readmission differences were too small to detect. Individual allocation on the postnatal ward is possible because monitoring happens at home. Remote monitoring closes the early measurement gap (c1), titration improved six-week control in a small trial (c3), readmission is underpowered (c2), and digital exclusion must be designed out (c4).

response.overview: Pragmatic trial with individual allocation on the postnatal ward, over 18 months, comparing remote blood pressure monitoring with midwife hub titration against usual community checks for women discharged after a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy.
response.population: Women aged 16 and over discharged after pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension who consent before discharge; women without a smartphone or needing an interpreter are included with a loan phone, a paper diary with hub calls, or interpreter calls.
response.exposure: A validated upper-arm monitor with a cuff sized at discharge; readings twice daily for two weeks, then daily to six weeks, sent by app, text or phone; hub midwives adjust medicines under protocol MAT-HTN-04 and call after high readings; out-of-hours severe readings go to the maternity assessment unit.
response.procedures: Allocation by a central web service after consent on the postnatal ward, stratified by pre-eclampsia versus gestational hypertension. Usual care continues in both arms. The six-week blood pressure is taken at the family doctor visit and retrieved from the shared record; readmissions from hospital records.

response.designSummary: Two-arm pragmatic trial with individual allocation stratified by diagnosis; binary primary outcome at six weeks.
response.sampleSize: Planning values from the retrieved self-management trial: 61 percent of usual-care women with blood pressure below 140 over 90 at six weeks, rounded to 60 percent, and 75 percent with remote monitoring. With 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05, about 152 women per arm are needed, 304 in total; allowing 10 percent missing six-week readings gives about 340. With about 412 eligible women a year and about 55 percent consenting, recruitment takes about 18 months, and the remote arm needs about 170 monitors, within the 300 funded. Readmission (about 9 percent locally) would need about 950 women to detect a halving and is reported descriptively.
response.primaryAnalysis: Logistic regression of control at six weeks on arm, adjusted for the stratification variable, intention to treat; risk difference with its 95 percent confidence interval.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Readmission or unplanned attendance and severe readings as risk differences with intervals; uptake and reporting by smartphone ownership and interpreter need, descriptive; burden and low blood pressure described by arm.
response.missingData: Missing six-week readings are handled by multiple imputation under missing at random, with a sensitivity analysis treating missing as uncontrolled.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary outcomes labelled as secondary with intervals.
response.software: R; statistical analysis plan archived before the first allocation.
overfittingGuards: One adjustment variable, the stratification factor

response.consent: Written informed consent on the postnatal ward before discharge, with interpreters and translated information; women can stop monitoring at any time and keep their usual care.
response.data: Readings are held on the app provider's platform under a data processing agreement and in the hub record; the analysis file uses study numbers.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: women without a smartphone, women needing an interpreter, younger mothers, recent migrants and women in deprived areas are the most likely to be excluded or to report less. Loan phones, paper diaries with hub calls and interpreter calls are part of the intervention, and outcomes are reported by digital access and language.
response.effectiveness: The trial is useful if it shows whether remote monitoring improves six-week control within the unit's own service and reaches women equally.

response.costs: Monitors, app licence and loan phones funded by the charity; hub midwife time within existing roles.
response.grants: None beyond the charity award; a positive result could support a larger trial powered for readmission.

response.title: Remote blood pressure monitoring with midwife-led titration after hypertensive pregnancy: a pragmatic trial
response.abstract: Objective: to test whether remote blood pressure monitoring with midwife hub titration and inclusive reporting options improves blood pressure control at six weeks after a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy. Design: pragmatic trial with individual allocation. Primary outcome: blood pressure below 140 over 90 at the six-week check. Results will follow the trial.
response.introduction: Blood pressure often peaks after discharge, when few women are measured. Retrieved trials show that remote monitoring closes this gap and may improve six-week control, but they excluded women without smartphones.
response.methods: Allocation after consent on the postnatal ward; validated monitors; app, text, paper or phone reporting; titration by protocol; routine six-week measurement; intention-to-treat analysis.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present recruitment by language and digital access, reporting adherence, the primary outcome with a risk difference, and secondary outcomes.
response.discussion: The discussion will weigh a surrogate primary outcome against the underpowered readmission outcome and consider who the intervention reached.
response.limitations: Surrogate primary outcome; unblinded; single unit.
response.conclusion: To be written after the trial.
